question_text: A research team skips agreeing on objectives and starts collecting data right away. Why is this risky?
hint: Think about what the first step does for every step that comes after it.

options.option_text: Research objectives are only set after data is analyzed.
options.option_explanation: The first step is to define the problem and agree on research objectives, before any data is collected.

options.option_text: Defining the problem is the easiest step to redo later.
options.option_explanation: Defining the problem is often the hardest step, not the easiest.

options.option_text: The first step guides the entire research process.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Defining the problem is often the hardest step, as it guides the entire research process.

options.option_text: Objectives only matter when the research is causal.
options.option_explanation: Objectives can be exploratory, descriptive, or causal. Every kind of research needs them.

prompt: A Montréal bakery chain is writing its research plan. Which part of the plan is each decision?

options.label: Cost against the value of insights

cases.text: The plan states that the team must learn which hours of the day bring the fewest customers into each shop.
cases.explanation: Pinning down exactly what the team needs to learn is the plan determining the exact information needed.

cases.text: The plan lists the chain's own till records and a city report on foot traffic as places to look first.
cases.explanation: Till records and a city report already exist. Listing them is outlining sources of existing data.

cases.text: The plan says the team will hand a short questionnaire to 300 customers at the counter.
cases.explanation: Saying how new information will be gathered spells out a specific research approach.

cases.text: A $40,000 study is dropped for a $3,000 one, because the answer will only change the opening hours of two shops.
cases.explanation: The plan weighs what the data costs against what the insights are worth to the decision.

cases.text: The plan states that the team must find the highest price customers would pay for a dozen croissants.
cases.explanation: A precise statement of what must be found out is the exact information needed.

cases.text: The plan says a researcher will stand in two shops and count how long people wait in line.
cases.explanation: This spells out how the data will be gathered: a specific research approach.

prompt: A sporting-goods retailer wants to know why winter-boot sales fell. Match each source of secondary data to what the retailer finds there.

pairs.match: Its own sales records from the last five winters
pairs.explanation: The records were kept for accounting, inside the company. They already exist, so they are internal secondary data.

pairs.match: Statistics Canada figures on household spending
pairs.explanation: A government agency published these figures for its own purposes. They already exist and can be relevant to the retailer's problem.

pairs.match: A market-research firm's report on footwear sales, sold to any buyer
pairs.explanation: A firm collects and sells this data to many clients. It is a commercial data service.

prompt: A coffee chain is gathering data. Sort each piece: is it primary data or secondary data?

cards.text: Answers from a taste test the chain runs this week on its new oat latte.
cards.explanation: The taste test is collected for the specific purpose at hand, so it is primary data.

cards.text: Census figures on how many people live near each café.
cards.explanation: The census already exists and was collected for another purpose. That makes it secondary data.

cards.text: Last year's sales receipts, kept for the accountants.
cards.explanation: The receipts already exist in an internal database, collected for another purpose.

cards.text: Interviews with 20 regulars about why they stopped buying muffins.
cards.explanation: The interviews are collected for this specific problem. That is primary data.

cards.text: A research firm's report on coffee trends that it sells to many companies.
cards.explanation: A commercial data service collected it for many buyers. It already exists, so it is secondary data.

cards.text: A count, taken by staff this morning, of how many customers order to go.
cards.explanation: Staff gathered it for the question at hand, so it is primary data.

prompt: Each case gathers primary data. Which research approach is it?

cases.text: A grocer films how shoppers move through the cereal aisle and where they stop.
cases.explanation: The grocer gathers data by observing relevant people and actions.

cases.text: A bank asks 1,000 students which credit cards they have heard of and how they feel about each one.
cases.explanation: Asking about knowledge and attitudes gathers descriptive information. That is survey research.

cases.text: A café sells a muffin at $3 in one shop and $4 in a matched shop, keeping everything else the same.
cases.explanation: Matched groups and controlled factors show whether the price causes a change in sales. That is causal information.

cases.text: A gym counts which machines members use most at each hour of the day.
cases.explanation: The gym watches what members do instead of asking them. That is observational research.

cases.text: An online store sends two matched groups the same email with different subject lines to see which one causes more clicks.
cases.explanation: Two matched groups, one factor changed: experimental research gathers causal information.

cases.text: A hotel emails guests a form asking them to rate their stay from 1 to 5.
cases.explanation: A rating form gathers descriptive information about attitudes. That is survey research.

question_text: A bank's sales, service, and marketing teams each keep separate notes on the same client and never share them. Which idea is the bank failing to apply?
hint: Which idea brings together everything the teams know about individual customers?

options.option_text: Experimental research, which matches groups and controls factors.
options.option_explanation: Experimental research gathers causal information. It does not combine what teams know about customers.

options.option_text: CRM, which integrates what those teams know about customers.
options.option_explanation: Correct. CRM manages detailed information about individual customers and integrates what sales, service, and marketing teams know.

options.option_text: Survey research, which gathers knowledge and attitudes.
options.option_explanation: Survey research gathers descriptive information. The bank's problem is unshared customer information.

options.option_text: Big Data, which refers to huge and complex data sets.
options.option_explanation: Big Data describes huge, complex data sets. The bank needs to integrate its teams' customer knowledge.

prompt: An online clothing store runs analytics on its data. Sort each finding: does it give a customer insight, or gauge marketing performance?

cards.text: Shoppers in Montréal buy rain jackets two days before a rainy forecast.
cards.explanation: A pattern in how customers behave is a customer insight.

cards.text: The spring email campaign brought 12% more visits than last spring's.
cards.explanation: Measuring what a campaign achieved gauges marketing performance.

cards.text: Customers who return one size usually reorder the next size up.
cards.explanation: This shows how customers act, so it is a customer insight.

cards.text: Each sale from video ads cost $9, against $4 from search ads.
cards.explanation: Comparing what each ad channel returns gauges marketing performance.

cards.text: Parents of young children mostly shop after 10 p.m. on their phones.
cards.explanation: A pattern in when and how a group of customers shops is a customer insight.

cards.text: The new homepage banner raised sales of the featured jacket by 20%.
cards.explanation: Checking the result of a marketing action gauges marketing performance.
